entries.hardening_notes: Test your WAF and input-validation controls against standard pattern collections in a lab, fix the application code so patterns are rejected by design (parameterized queries, output encoding), and keep signatures updated. Test only systems you own.
entries.attack_profile: Payloads are the malicious inputs attackers deliver to vulnerable sinks: injection strings, traversal sequences, and command fragments tailored to each flaw class. Conceptually the payload is the attacker's voice speaking the application's own language against it. Targets: databases, file systems, and operating-system shells behind the app. Observable footprints: pattern matches in WAF and application logs, especially encoded variants.

entries.name: PayloadsAllTheThings
entries.defensive_summary: PayloadsAllTheThings is a large collection of payload patterns and bypass techniques for web application security testing. Defenders use it the way vaccine researchers use virus samples: to test and strengthen controls in authorized assessments. Each bypass documented is a gap to close in your WAF rules and input handling.
entries.detection_notes: Watch for bypass-pattern variations in logs that evade your current signatures; each evasion is a signature-improvement task. Correlate multi-vector probing from single sources as targeted assessment activity.
entries.hardening_notes: Validate WAF rules against bypass collections in a lab, fix applications so bypasses fail at the code level rather than relying on the WAF alone, and layer controls so no single bypass defeats the defense. Restrict testing to authorized systems.
entries.attack_profile: This collection documents bypass thinking: when a defense blocks the obvious payload, attackers mutate it — encoding, alternative syntax, and filter-evasion tricks — until something slips through. Conceptually it is an arms race between filter and filter-evasion. Targets: input filters, WAFs, and sanitizers. Observable footprints: multi-vector probing from single sources and filter-evasion patterns in logs.

entries.name: Pentest Wiki
entries.defensive_summary: Pentest Wiki is a free knowledge library documenting penetration-testing methodology for researchers. Defenders study assessment methodology to understand how their environment would be attacked: the enumeration order, the privilege-escalation paths, the exfiltration routes. Methodology knowledge directs hardening to the paths attackers actually walk.
entries.detection_notes: Map documented assessment methodologies to your telemetry: each methodology phase should correspond to detections in your environment. Silent phases are your detection roadmap.
entries.hardening_notes: Harden along the paths methodology documents: enumeration resistance, privilege boundaries, and egress controls. Use the methodology as a checklist for your own authorized assessments, then remediate by root cause.
entries.attack_profile: Documented assessment methodology describes the standard attack progression: enumerate, gain foothold, escalate, move laterally, persist, exfiltrate. Conceptually methodology turns scattered techniques into a repeatable campaign plan. Targets: the full environment. Observable footprints: methodology phases map directly to detection opportunities at each stage.

entries.name: Probable Wordlists
entries.defensive_summary: Probable Wordlists are password lists ordered by real-world probability, originally built for password research. Defenders use them to measure password strength honestly: if a password appears early in a probability-ordered list, it will fall quickly. They turn password policy from guesswork into measurement.
entries.detection_notes: Watch authentication logs for guessing patterns that follow probability-ordered attempts, which indicate list-driven attacks rather than random brute force. Alert on high-velocity attempts against many accounts.
entries.hardening_notes: Screen new passwords against probability-ordered lists at creation time, require MFA so even guessed passwords are insufficient, and enforce length minimums that push passwords beyond practical guessing. Never use these lists against accounts you do not own.
entries.attack_profile: Probability-ordered guessing attacks try the most likely passwords first, making short work of human-chosen secrets: credential stuffing replays breached pairs, spraying tries few passwords across many accounts. Conceptually the attack exploits the predictability of human memory. Targets: password-only accounts. Observable footprints: high-velocity logon attempts following probability order and bursts across many usernames.

entries.name: Red Team Physical Tools
entries.defensive_summary: Red Team Physical Tools covers the equipment used in physical security assessments: access-control testing and covert-entry gear. Defenders study this domain to harden the physical layer that technical controls assume: badge systems, locks, and facility procedures. A network is only as secure as the building it sits in.
entries.detection_notes: Watch badge-access logs for tailgating indicators, after-hours access anomalies, and cloned-credential use. Correlate physical access events with logical access for the same identity.
entries.hardening_notes: Enforce anti-tailgating procedures and test them, use badge systems with cloning-resistant credentials, and run authorized physical assessments to find weaknesses before adversaries do. Train staff to challenge unknown individuals politely.
entries.attack_profile: Physical attacks bypass digital controls entirely: cloning badge credentials, tailgating through secured doors, and accessing exposed network ports or unlocked workstations. Conceptually the building's trust assumptions are the vulnerability. Targets: facility access leading to network access. Observable footprints: badge anomalies, after-hours access, and unknown devices on internal ports.

entries.name: Reverse Engineering
entries.defensive_summary: Reverse Engineering is the systematic analysis of software to understand its inner workings, covered here through articles, books, and papers. Defenders rely on it for malware analysis, vulnerability research, and verifying third-party components. Deep reverse-engineering skill produces the precise, behavior-based detections that signatures alone cannot.
entries.detection_notes: Analysts trained in reverse engineering produce higher-quality indicators: behaviors that survive malware repacking rather than fragile hashes. Track whether dissections yield detections within the incident timeline.
entries.hardening_notes: Invest in analyst training and lab tooling for binary analysis, document findings as reusable detection logic, and use reverse-engineering insights to harden the specific platforms and formats attackers target.
entries.attack_profile: Reverse engineering of malicious software exposes attacker tradecraft: how command-and-control protocols are structured, how persistence is implemented, and which evasion checks the malware performs. Conceptually it converts an opaque binary into a documented adversary capability. Targets: understanding, for defense. Footprints produced: network indicators, host artifacts, and behavioral signatures.

entries.name: RFSec-ToolKit
entries.defensive_summary: RFSec-ToolKit collects tools for analyzing radio-frequency communication protocols. Defenders care because wireless is invisible: rogue access points, vulnerable IoT radios, and insecure RF protocols all operate below the view of wired monitoring. RF awareness closes a blind spot.
entries.detection_notes: Watch for rogue wireless access points, unexpected RF protocol traffic near facilities, and wireless intrusion-detection alerts. Baseline the authorized RF environment so anomalies are visible.
entries.hardening_notes: Deploy wireless intrusion detection, enforce WPA3 with strong credentials on corporate wireless, and segment IoT radios from sensitive networks. Survey facilities periodically for unauthorized transmitters.
entries.attack_profile: RF attacks target wireless protocols: rogue access points for interception, deauthentication to force reconnections, and exploitation of weak IoT radio protocols. Conceptually radio is a shared medium where the loudest transmitter wins trust. Targets: wireless credentials and device control. Observable footprints: rogue access-point beacons, deauthentication floods, and unknown transmitters.

entries.name: Security Cheatsheets
entries.defensive_summary: Security Cheatsheets distill defensive best practices into concise, actionable guidance, notably the OWASP Cheat Sheet Series for application security. Defenders care because cheatsheets convert expert knowledge into checklists developers and operators can actually follow. They are among the highest-leverage defensive documents in existence.
entries.detection_notes: Use cheatsheets as audit baselines: check whether your applications and configurations match the recommended practices, and treat deviations as findings. Track adoption per team.
entries.hardening_notes: Adopt the relevant cheatsheets as organizational standards, integrate them into code review checklists and configuration baselines, and update them as the sheets evolve. Prefer concise, actionable guidance over long policy documents.

entries.name: Shell
entries.defensive_summary: Shell covers command-line frameworks, toolkits, and guides for making full use of the terminal. Defenders live in the shell: log analysis, incident response, and automation all run through it. Shell fluency multiplies every other defensive skill, and understanding shell tradecraft helps recognize malicious shell use.
entries.detection_notes: Watch for shells spawned from unusual parents (office documents, web servers), encoded command lines, and interactive shells on servers that should not have them. Command-line logging is one of the highest-value telemetry sources.
entries.hardening_notes: Enable command-line logging everywhere, restrict interactive shell access with jump hosts and MFA, and train responders in shell-based triage. Build response tooling as auditable scripts, not ad-hoc commands.
entries.attack_profile: Malicious shell use is the universal post-exploitation language: encoded commands to evade logging, shells spawned from exploited applications, and living-off-the-land binaries for every phase. Conceptually the shell turns any foothold into full system control. Targets: the host and everything reachable from it. Observable footprints: shells with unusual parents, encoded command lines, and interactive sessions on servers.

entries.name: Suricata
entries.defensive_summary: Suricata is an open-source IDS/IPS and network security monitoring engine. Defenders deploy it to inspect network traffic for malicious patterns in real time, with protocol awareness far beyond simple string matching. Properly tuned, it is a cornerstone of network detection.
entries.detection_notes: Watch Suricata alert telemetry for rule hits correlated with endpoint and log data, and track rule performance to prune noisy signatures. Alert on Suricata sensor health itself: a blind sensor is a coverage gap.
entries.hardening_notes: Deploy sensors at network choke points with adequate hardware, tune rules to your traffic to control false positives, and update rulesets on a schedule. Run in IDS mode first to validate before enabling IPS blocking.

entries.name: ThreatHunter-Playbook
entries.defensive_summary: ThreatHunter-Playbook provides structured hypotheses and techniques for proactive threat hunting. Defenders care because hunting finds the intrusions that automated alerts miss: analysts start from adversary behavior and search telemetry for it. A playbook turns hunting from art into repeatable process.
entries.detection_notes: Track hunt outcomes: confirmed true positives become permanent detections, and hunts that find nothing still validate coverage. Measure mean dwell time of hunt-discovered intrusions.
entries.hardening_notes: Run hunts on a schedule driven by your threat model, document every hunt as a hypothesis with data sources and findings, and convert successful hunts into automated detections. Ensure hunts have access to the telemetry they need.

entries.name: Tor
entries.defensive_summary: Tor covers the anonymity network and its implications for defenders. Defenders care because Tor is dual-use: it protects legitimate privacy, and it also carries malicious traffic that bypasses normal attribution. Organizations need a deliberate Tor policy rather than accidental exposure.
entries.detection_notes: Watch for Tor client traffic on corporate networks, connections to known Tor entry nodes, and data exfiltration patterns routed through anonymity networks. Decide whether Tor use is alert-worthy or policy-violating in your environment.
entries.hardening_notes: Define an explicit organizational policy on Tor, block or allow Tor at the boundary per that policy, and monitor for circumvention. Harden any legitimate Tor use cases with endpoint controls and logging.
entries.attack_profile: Tor abuse leverages anonymity for malicious ends: exfiltrating data through onion routing, operating command-and-control that resists takedown, and obscuring attacker origin. Conceptually the same properties that protect legitimate privacy also protect intruders. Targets: attribution itself. Observable footprints: Tor client traffic on corporate networks and connections to entry nodes during incidents.

entries.name: Vulhub
entries.defensive_summary: Vulhub provides pre-built vulnerable environments for practicing exploitation and defense in isolated containers. Defenders use these environments to reproduce real CVEs safely: confirm patch effectiveness, develop detections for the exploitation pattern, and train responders on real vulnerability mechanics. Reproducing the flaw is the fastest path to understanding it.
entries.detection_notes: For each reproduced CVE, capture the exploitation telemetry and verify your detections fire on it. Track which reproduced vulnerabilities lack detection coverage in production.
entries.hardening_notes: Run vulnerable environments strictly isolated and never expose them to untrusted networks, use them to validate patches before production rollout, and tear them down after exercises. Convert each exercise into a detection or hardening note.

entries.name: Web Security
entries.defensive_summary: Web Security curates materials on securing web applications and infrastructure. Defenders care because the web remains the dominant attack surface: nearly every breach involves a web vector somewhere. A current, curated reading list keeps defenders aligned with how web attacks evolve.
entries.detection_notes: Stay current on emerging web attack classes and verify your logging captures the data needed to detect them. Review WAF and application logs against newly documented techniques.
entries.hardening_notes: Maintain a web-security baseline covering headers, TLS, authentication, and input handling, review it against current materials annually, and test applications with authorized assessments. Patch web stacks on a disciplined cadence.
entries.attack_profile: Web attack classes evolve continuously: new injection variants, client-side attacks on single-page apps, and supply-chain compromises of frontend dependencies. Conceptually the web's complexity guarantees a steady supply of trust-boundary mistakes. Targets: users and their data via the browser and the server. Observable footprints: emerging probe patterns that defenders must learn to recognize.
